"You look at problems through one lens. Many computations are a loop: the next state is computed from the current one,
so step 1,000 cannot start until step 999 ends, and when the state is small most of a GPU sits idle. Such a loop can
sometimes be computed all at once: guess every state, check every step in parallel against the one before, correct
all the errors together, and repeat until nothing changes. The result is exactly what the loop would give. It pays only
when the system forgets its past, so that early errors fade: damped, dissipative or mixing dynamics, or a long sampling
chain. It fails when small errors grow, as in chaotic systems. Before spending, measure forgetfulness: start two runs a
hair apart and see whether they converge or drift apart. A good candidate has a step-by-step loop, a small state (a
handful to a few hundred numbers), a long run (thousands of steps or more), forgetful dynamics, and few runs needed; if
thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead. The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how
long one answer takes. Before proposing anything, check whether a strong GPU method for this already exists; rebuilding
it wins nothing. Write down your predictions and how you could be wrong before any test, and compare against a tuned
sequential baseline and against many independent copies run side by side.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: generative pipeline for discovery of single phase immersion coolants
Problem:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me parse the task. The user gives a "reframe" prompt context: a lens about parallel-in-time / speculative computation being useful only for forgetful dynamics, etc. Then a research problem: IC-V1, force-field error floor for coolant MD, Green–Kubo MD on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters, ranking viscosity and thermal conductivity against measurements, benchmark 8→120 molecules, hypothesis of chemistry-dependent error floor ~25%.

Task: "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost."

Return JSON with schema: reframes array, each with fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior.

So I need to produce up to three reframes. Let me think about the problem deeply.

The problem: Green–Kubo MD with fixed force field (LOPLS-AA) has error floor ~25% for viscosity/thermal conductivity of C10–C50 molecules at 40°C. The plan is to scale from 8 to 120 molecules to check if error is correctable bias or random floor. Compute axis is just more molecules — more of the same. If the error floor is force-field systematic, more molecules don't help ranking; more replicas don't help either (GK noise averages out but bias remains). The bottleneck: fixed force field error is systematic; more sampling/more molecules measures the floor but doesn't reduce it.

Where does more compute stop helping? Once you've got 6×5ns replicas per molecule, statistical error in GK is small compared to force-field bias; adding molecules only estimates the bias distribution, doesn't change per-molecule predictions. So compute buys more of the same.

Reframings that would let more compute change the answer:

1. Change the unit of work from "molecule" to "force-field parameter fit": use compute to re-fit or correct the force field (e.g., per-molecule polarizable charges from DFT, or machine-learned corrections / Δ-learning) so that more compute actually reduces error rather than measures it. Question: does a DFT-derived charge refit per molecule (e.g., RESP charges at HF/6-31G*) reduce held-out viscosity error below 15%? Cheapest measurement: pick ~12 molecules spanning the error range, compute DFT charges, run short GK (2×2ns), compare viscosity error vs LOPLS-AA stock charges. Cost: DFT charges for 12 molecules ~ tens of CPU-hours; MD ~ a few GPU-hours; maybe $10–30.

2. Change what is measured: instead of equilibrium Green–Kubo (which needs long trajectories and has noisy integrals for thermal conductivity), use reverse non-equilibrium MD (rNEMD) which gives lower variance per unit time for viscosity and thermal conductivity — more compute then buys precision that changes ranking rather than noise. Question: does rNEMD at matched compute reduce the confidence interval on viscosity enough that rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 at 24 molecules? Cheapest measurement: run rNEMD and GK on the 8 published molecules at equal GPU-hours, compare standard errors. Cost ~ $5–15.

3. Change the objective/order of steps: instead of ranking absolute transport properties against measurement (capped by force-field floor), rank pairs (differential ranking) or predict within-homologous-series ordering where systematic errors cancel. Or: use compute to estimate the bias as a function of chemistry (chain length, ester vs hydrocarbon) from the 8 known molecules, fit a correction model, then test on held-out molecules — compute spent on a bias-model cross-validation rather than more raw molecules. Question: does a two-parameter correction (chain length × chemistry class) fitted on 8 molecules bring held-out viscosity error under 15% on 16 new molecules? Cheapest measurement: run GK on 16 molecules with existing protocol, fit correction on the published 8, score. Cost ~ $20–40.

Alternatively a reframe aligned with the "lens" preamble: the preamble is about parallel-in-time methods for forgetful dynamics. Hmm — the system prompt prefix is the "one lens" text about parallel-in-time (Parareal-like) methods. The task says "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping... reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer." The lens is given as context for how to think about compute levers. For MD: each molecule's trajectory is a sequential loop, but dynamics are mixing/forgetful (liquids), and there are many independent replicas/molecules — so the right move is running them side by side (embarrassingly parallel), which the plan already does (replicas). The preamble also says "check whether a strong GPU method already exists" — for GK MD, LAMMPS on GPU is standard; rNEMD is the lower-variance alternative.

So reframes could also include: the unit of work is "one long trajectory" — but GK needs long autocorrelation; since liquid dynamics are mixing (forgetful), one long run can be replaced by many short independent runs giving the same statistics; that changes wall time, not total compute — but the problem already uses replicas. The true bottleneck is the force-field floor, not sampling. So the reframes should focus on breaking the floor.

Let me craft three reframes:

Reframe 1 — Bottleneck: error floor is a force-field bias; more molecules measure it, don't reduce it. Assumption: the LOPLS-AA parameter set is fixed and the bias must be accepted. Reframe: change the unit of work from "molecule simulated with fixed FF" to "candidate FF variant/correction evaluated"; spend compute on per-molecule DFT-derived charges (or a small set of FF perturbations) so added compute can actually lower the error, not just characterize it. Question: does re-deriving atomic charges per molecule (DFT RESP) cut held-out viscosity error below 15% on a 12-molecule span? Measure: cheapest: 12 molecules (6 hydrocarbons, 6 esters spanning C10–C50 and the published error range), DFT single-point + RESP (~hours of CPU), 2×3ns GK each on one GPU; compare |error| vs stock LOPLS-AA on same trajectories length. Cost ~ $25. compute_after: if it works, scale to 120 molecules + refit LJ params; compute directly reduces error. exact: hmm, "exact" field — probably means the exact measurement/quantity? The schema fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior. I need to interpret these. Likely from the metis "reframe" template: "exact" = the exact measurement (what exactly is measured), "expected" = expected outcome, "fails_if" = the falsification condition, "closest_prior" = nearest prior work. So "exact" might be "the exact quantity measured" e.g., "held-out mean absolute percent error in viscosity at 40 °C vs measured values from the 835-molecule reference set". And "measure" = description of the cheapest measurement procedure, with cost. Hmm, both measure and exact... Perhaps "measure" is the cheapest measurement to answer the question and "exact" is the precise quantitative definition / pass criterion. I'll fill accordingly: measure = procedure + rough cost; exact = the precise metric and threshold; expected = what you expect to see; fails_if = condition under which the reframe is dead; closest_prior = the nearest existing work (from the text: Ogbomo 8-molecule GK MD; or known literature: rNEMD Müller-Plathe; DFT charge refits for LOPLS; etc.).

Reframe 2 — Bottleneck: GK equilibrium noise for thermal conductivity requires long trajectories; precision per GPU-hour is low, so the plan spends most budget reducing noise that isn't the binding constraint, and ranking is limited by bias + noise combination. Assumption: equilibrium GK is the estimator. Reframe: change what is measured/how it's measured: switch estimator to reverse-NEMD (Müller-Plathe), which gives several-fold lower variance for viscosity and thermal conductivity at the same compute; extra compute then buys rank precision on more molecules instead of marginally shrinking error bars. Question: at equal GPU-hours, does rNEMD halve the standard error of viscosity and thermal conductivity vs GK on the published 8 molecules? Measure: run rNEMD and GK on the 8 published molecules at matched GPU-hours (~4 GPU-hours each), compare bootstrap SEs; ~$10. compute_after: if SE per dollar is ≥2× better, reallocate the whole 120-molecule budget to rNEMD, doubling effective sample or halving cost. exact: ratio of standard errors at fixed compute. fails_if: rNEMD SE ratio < 1.3× (not worth retooling) or rNEMD bias differs from GK by more than its SE. closest_prior: Müller-Plathe rNEMD viscosity/thermal conductivity literature; the Ogbomo study used GK only [s_ogbomo_md].

Reframe 3 — Bottleneck: objective is absolute agreement with measurement, capped by chemistry-dependent bias; rank correlation across all chemistries is the casualty. Assumption: ranking must use raw simulated values against measurement. Reframe: change the objective/order: fit a bias model on a small calibration set (or use within-class differential ranking, e.g., chain-length ordering) so systematic components cancel; compute then goes to estimating the correction and validating held-out rank, where more molecules actually improve the answer (shrink correction uncertainty). Question: does a two- or three-parameter chemistry-conditioned correction fitted on the published 8 molecules bring held-out viscosity MAPE below 15% and Spearman ρ above 0.9 on 16 held-out molecules? Measure: run GK (existing protocol, can reuse replicas) on 16 molecules chosen to cover the correction's axes (chain length × ester/hydrocarbon), fit correction on Ogbomo's 8, score held-out; ~24 GPU-hours ≈ $30. compute_after: if it holds, scale held-out set to 60–120 molecules; each added molecule tightens the correction and tests generality — compute changes the answer. fails_if: held-out error stays ≥25% or ρ ≤0.7 regardless of correction, i.e., bias is not a smooth function of the chosen descriptors. closest_prior: Ogbomo 8-molecule bias patterns (density within 4%, κ over-predicted for all 8) [s_ogbomo_res].

Alternative reframe aligned with the preamble's parallel-in-time lens: The preamble suggests checking whether the loop is forgetful and whether many independent runs side-by-side is better — the MD already does that; a reframe could be: replace long single trajectories with many short trajectories started from decorrelated snapshots because liquid momentum/energy flux autocorrelation is forgetful; more compute then buys many independent short runs (side by side) reducing wall time and letting per-molecule cost drop, enabling 835 molecules. But that's essentially "more of the same" — though it changes the unit of work from "6×5ns replicas" to "many 0.5ns runs," exploiting forgetfulness. Question: does the Green–Kubo integral from 60×0.5 ns decorrelated starts match 6×5 ns within statistical error, at better GPU utilization? Measure: on 2 molecules, compare both estimators; ~$5. That is a legit reframe and directly uses the lens. But is it one of the top three? The plan's cost is $940 over 59 machine-hours; if short-run parallelism reduces wall-time but total compute is the same, it doesn't change the answer, just speed. The preamble says: "The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how long one answer takes." And "if thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead" — already done. Hmm. I think the three reframes above (FF refit, estimator change, objective change) are stronger. But maybe include the sampling-unit reframe instead of one? Let me rank by "would let more compute change the answer":

1. FF correction/refit (compute reduces error directly) — strong.
2. Bias-model calibration objective (more molecules improve correction and held-out validation) — strong; note the original plan already frames "bias correction" in "If compute is the lever": "held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent". So the plan already includes bias correction! Interesting: "If compute is the lever. At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent..." So they already anticipate bias correction. Then reframe 3 is partially anticipated. Still, the reframe could sharpen it: fit the correction on the published 8 first (cheap) before buying 120 molecules — reorder steps: calibrate early, then scale only if the correction generalizes. That's an "order of steps" reframe and could save $900. Good.

3. Estimator change (rNEMD) — changes precision per dollar; does it "change the answer"? If the floor is bias, no. But it changes whether noise masks rank at fixed budget; and if the bias turns out correctable, better precision per dollar means more molecules per dollar (maybe all 835). It's a "unit of work" reframe. Decent.

4. Change what is measured: instead of viscosity/κ absolute values, measure the quantities the force field gets right by construction (density, enthalpy of vaporization) and use them to select/repair FF before transport; or measure at multiple temperatures to get activation energy of viscosity (rank by ΔE rather than absolute η) — systematic errors may cancel in derivatives. Question: does ranking by simulated viscosity activation energy (η at 25/40/60 °C) match measured ranking better than absolute η at 40 °C? Measure: run GK at 3 temperatures on 8 molecules, compare Spearman ρ of activation energy vs measured; ~$15. That's a genuine "change what is measured" reframe.

Also "check whether a strong GPU method already exists": rNEMD in LAMMPS exists; also machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) — e.g., train a Δ-ML potential on DFT for a few molecules; that's expensive. The DFT charge refit is the cheap version.

Let me settle on three reframes:

A. Unit of work: fixed-FF molecule → per-molecule charge-refit (DFT/RESP) molecule; compute can cut the bias itself. Question: per-molecule RESP charges cut held-out viscosity error under 15% on 12 molecules spanning the known bias?

B. Order of steps + objective: fit the chemistry-conditioned bias correction on the already-published 8 molecules and validate on the cheapest next 16 before buying 120; compute then buys correction generality rather than more floor-mapping. Question: does a correction fit on 8 generalize to 16 held-out molecules (viscosity MAPE < 15%, Spearman ρ > 0.9)?

C. What is measured/how: swap estimator (rNEMD) and/or measured quantity (temperature derivative of viscosity) so extra compute buys rank-relevant signal instead of noise around a biased mean. Question: at equal GPU-hours, does rNEMD (or the 3-temperature viscosity slope) give Spearman ρ ≥ 0.9 against measurement where GK absolute values give ≤ 0.7? Hmm, mixing two ideas in one reframe is muddy. Better to pick one. The prompt says up to three reframes; each should be crisp. I'll choose:

C. What is measured: rank by temperature-dependence (viscosity activation energy / slope) instead of absolute 40 °C values — systematic force-field errors that scale with chemistry may cancel in the derivative, so compute spent at extra temperatures changes the ranking answer rather than re-measuring the floor. Cheapest measurement: run the existing protocol at 25 and 60 °C on the published 8 molecules (2 extra state points × 8 molecules × 6×5ns ≈ 16 GPU-hours ≈ $20), compute Spearman ρ of simulated vs measured viscosity-temperature slope. Fails if rank correlation of slopes is no better than of absolute values (ρ improvement < 0.1).

Alternatively C could be rNEMD. Which is more compelling given "the plan expects: not the lever"? The problem statement says "plan expects: not the lever" — i.e., compute is expected not to be the lever, and PASS. So the meta-context: this seed expects compute not to help; the reframe exercise is to find changes that would make compute help. The strongest reframe is the one that attacks the force-field floor with compute (A), since the hypothesis says the floor is FF-driven. B reorders to cheaply kill or confirm. C changes the measured quantity.

I might also consider: unit of work change to "ML potential fine-tuned per chemistry class" — but that's expensive and "check first whether a strong GPU method exists" — MLIPs for hydrocarbons exist (e.g., ANI, MACE fine-tuning). The DFT-charge refit is the cheapest version of "spend compute on the physics, not the sampling." Keep A as is.

Costs: need rough costs consistent with the budget language: plan $940.98 over 59 machine-hours → ~$16/machine-hour (GPU-hour ~ $16? seems high; but fine, it's their number; 59 machine-hours for 8 GPUs maybe; $940.98/59 ≈ $15.95/hr). I'll just give rough dollar costs in that spirit: A ~$30–40 (DFT charges CPU + 24 short GK runs ≈ 6 GPU-hours... let me estimate: 12 molecules × 2×3 ns; at the plan's throughput guess, a 5 ns replica costs ~$940/(120×6)... actually plan: 120 molecules × 6 replicas × 5 ns = 3600 replica-runs for $940 → ~$0.26 per 5-ns replica? That seems too cheap. 59 machine-hours for 3600 replicas → 16 replicas per machine-hour — implausible unless "machine-hours" means something else. Whatever — rough costs: A: 12 molecules × 4 replicas × 3ns ≈ maybe 10 GPU-hours ≈ $20–50. I'll say "~$30". B: 16 molecules × 6×5ns ≈ same as plan's per-molecule cost ×16: plan says 8→24→48→120 for $940; 16 molecules ≈ $40–60. Say ~$50. C: 8 molecules × 2 extra temps × 6×5ns = 96 replicas ≈ 16/120 of plan? Plan does 120×6=720 replicas for $940 → 96 replicas ≈ $125. Hmm, that math: 8+24+48+120=200 molecules ×6 =1200 replicas for $940 → ~$0.78/replica → 96 replicas ≈ $75. Say ~$75, or reduce to 3 replicas per temp → ~$40. I'll say ~$40–75, give a single rough number ~$50.

Actually keep numbers loose: "≈$30", "≈$50", "≈$60". Fine.

Also each reframe needs "exact" — I'll interpret as the exact pass/fail measurement definition (the precise number to compare). And "expected" — what you'd expect if the reframe is right. "fails_if" — kill condition. "closest_prior" — nearest prior work; from the text: [s_ogbomo_md] (8-molecule GK study) is the anchor; I can also cite generic known things (Müller-Plathe 1997 rNEMD; standard RESP/AM1-BCC charge practice in OPLS/GAFF). The instruction says "Decide from the text above and what you know" — so referencing known literature is fine, but keep it plausible and non-fabricated in specifics. I'll cite names/years only where well-established: Müller-Plathe reverse NEMD (1997); OPLS-AA/LOPLS with fixed CM1/CM5 charges; RESP (Bayly et al. 1993). For the reframe C (temperature slope), closest prior is the Ogbomo 8-molecule single-temperature study — i.e., closest prior measured only 40 °C.

Field "compute_after": what compute looks like after the reframe / how much and what it buys. E.g., A: "If charges cut error, scale to 120 molecules: 120 DFT charge derivations + 720 replicas ≈ $950 (same budget) but error floor moves with spend." B: "Only if the 8→16 correction generalizes, buy the remaining 104 molecules (~$800) to tighten and validate the correction; otherwise stop at ~$50." C: "If slope ranking holds, full campaign becomes 3 temperatures × 120 molecules ≈ 3× plan (~$2,800) or same budget over 40 molecules; spend buys rank-relevant signal."

Let me also write the "bottleneck" for each:

A. Bottleneck: "The error floor lives in the fixed LOPLS-AA parameters, not in sampling; once GK noise is below the bias (already true at 6×5 ns), every added molecule or replica only re-measures the same chemistry-dependent bias — more compute buys more of the same."

B. Bottleneck: "Steps are ordered biggest-spend-first on the raw property; the plan buys 120 molecules before knowing whether any bias correction generalizes, so compute is spent mapping the floor rather than testing whether it can be removed." Assumption: "Bias correction must be validated at 120 molecules; the published 8 cannot support a correction model." Reframe: reorder — fit the correction on the published 8 (zero new MD), validate on the cheapest informative held-out set (16 molecules chosen on the correction axes), scale only if it generalizes.

C. Bottleneck: "What is measured — absolute η and κ at one temperature — is exactly where the force field is worst; rank information is swamped by a chemistry-dependent offset that no amount of 40 °C sampling removes."

Assumption C: "Absolute 40 °C values are the quantity that must rank."

Reframe C: "Change the measured quantity to the temperature response (viscosity slope/activation energy from 25–60 °C, and κ ratio), where multiplicative force-field errors largely cancel; compute at extra temperatures buys new signal instead of re-measuring a biased constant."

Question C: "Does the Spearman rank correlation between simulated and measured viscosity temperature-slope (log η vs 1/T over 25–60 °C) on the 8 published molecules exceed the 0.7 ceiling that absolute 40 °C values cannot break?"

Hmm — but is it known absolute values give ρ<0.7 at 8 molecules? The "If not" branch says rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size. Fine to phrase as "exceed 0.9 where absolute values sit below 0.7".

Expected C: "Slope ranks correctly for 7–8 of 8 molecules; ρ ≥ 0.9, because the dominant FF error is a prefactor."

Fails_if C: "Simulated slopes show ρ ≤ 0.7 vs measurement, or the simulated activation energies are near-constant across molecules (no discriminating signal) — then the offset is not a simple prefactor and the reframe is dead."

Measure C: "Reuse the published 8-molecule protocol at 25 and 60 °C (6×5 ns each; 8×2×6=96 replicas ≈ 15 GPU-hours, ≈$60); regress log η vs 1/T per molecule; compare Spearman ρ of simulated vs measured slopes against the ρ from 40 °C absolutes."

Exact C: "Spearman ρ between simulated and measured d(log η)/d(1/T) over the 8 molecules, vs ρ between simulated and measured η(40 °C); success = slope-ρ ≥ 0.9 and ≥ 0.2 above absolute-ρ."

Closest_prior C: "Ogbomo 2026 single-temperature (40 °C) GK benchmark on the same 8 molecules [s_ogbomo_md]; no multi-temperature scoring in the reference set [s_ogbomo_db]."

Now A details:

Assumption A: "The LOPLS-AA parameter set — especially its fixed, generic partial charges — must be taken as given; the floor is a fact to be measured, not a bias to be repaired."

Reframe A: "Change the unit of work from 'molecule at fixed force field' to 'force-field variant per molecule': derive per-molecule RESP/AM1-BCC-style charges from a cheap DFT single point and rerun short GK; if the error drops, additional compute (more molecules, then LJ refits or Δ-ML corrections) directly lowers the floor instead of documenting it."

Question A: "On 12 molecules spanning C10–C50 and both chemistries, do per-molecule DFT-derived charges (HF/6-31G* RESP) cut held-out viscosity MAPE below 15% where stock LOPLS-AA charges give ~25%?"

Measure A: "12 molecules (6 hydrocarbons + 6 esters chosen from the published set's high- and low-error ends): DFT single point + RESP fit per molecule (~1 CPU-hour each, ≈$5 total), then 2×3 ns GK per molecule at 40 °C on one GPU (≈6–8 GPU-hours, ≈$30); score viscosity |error| vs stock charges on identical sampling. ≈$35, a few days wall time."

Compute_after A: "If the charge refit clears 15%, spend the full budget on 120 refits + LJ correction fit (~$950, same envelope) where each added dollar reduces error; if partial, escalate to class-specific LJ refit or Δ-ML before any 120-molecule raw run."

Exact A: "Per-molecule |η_sim − η_meas|/η_meas at 40 °C, averaged over the 12, with stock vs refit charges at identical sampling; success = refit MAPE ≤ 15% and ≥ 10 percentage points below stock."

Expected A: "Esters improve most (their polarity is where generic charges err); MAPE falls from ~25% to ~12–18%; sign of the viscosity bias flips or shrinks in ≥ 8 of 12 molecules."

Fails_if A: "Refit MAPE stays ≥ 20%, or improvement < 5 points — then the floor sits in LJ/dispersion or in the dynamics assumptions, not charges, and per-molecule refits are not the lever."

Closest_prior A: "Ogbomo 2026 ran stock LOPLS-AA only [s_ogbomo_md]; charge derivation (RESP, Bayly 1993) is standard practice in OPLS/GAFF parameterization but was not varied in the benchmark [s_ogbomo_res]."

B details:

Bottleneck B: "The plan spends ~$940 mapping an error floor it already hypothesizes (25%, chemistry-dependent); validation of the only thing that could move the answer — whether a bias correction generalizes — is deferred to the largest, last set size."

Assumption B: "A bias correction can only be fitted and validated once 120 molecules are in hand; small calibration sets cannot support it."

Reframe B: "Invert the order: fit a small chemistry-conditioned correction (chain length × ester/hydrocarbon, 2–4 parameters) on the already-published 8 molecules at zero MD cost, then buy the cheapest discriminating held-out set (16 molecules at the corners of the correction axes) before committing to 48 or 120. More molecules now buy correction generality — a different answer — rather than a finer map of the same floor."

Question B: "Does a ≤4-parameter correction fitted only on Ogbomo's 8 molecules hold on 16 held-out molecules — held-out viscosity MAPE ≤ 15% and Spearman ρ ≥ 0.9 against measurement?"

Measure B: "Select 16 molecules at the extremes of chain length × chemistry from the 835-set; run the existing protocol (6×5 ns, ≈$3–4/molecule at plan throughput ≈ $55 total); fit correction on the published 8, apply frozen to the 16, score. ≈$60, ~1 week."

Compute_after B: "If it generalizes, the remaining 104 molecules (~$800) each tighten the correction and extend its domain — compute changes predictions; if it fails, stop at ~$60 instead of $940."
